title: Harrison's Sea Clock: How Many Miles Off, and How Was the Longitude Prize Paid?
description:
In 1765, the British Parliament wrote the results of John Harrison's sea clock trial into an Act. How many miles was the watch off after crossing the Atlantic? And why did the Act also demand that its construction be made public and that more timekeepers like it be built? This episode runs from the 1714 Longitude prize and his son William's two voyages to the West Indies, to the prize conditions of 1765, Harrison's public protest against the testing in 1767, and the further reward of 1773.

The main sources are fixed OCR editions of the British Acts of Parliament of 1765 and 1773, and Harrison's 1767 pamphlet. The Act's "geographical miles" are roughly nautical miles; ten miles is the trial result Parliament recorded, and this episode did not recalculate the original logbooks. Harrison's criticism of the Board and of Maskelyne is his own account, not treated as an independent verdict. The King's intervention, mentioned in the topic proposal, was not found in the originals read for this episode, so it is left out. The illustrations are AI-generated cartoons for illustration only; they do not reconstruct the exact H4 movement or legible documents.

Information as of 2026-10-19.

hs001.text: In 1765, Parliament wrote the results of Harrison's sea clock trial into an Act.

hs002.text: The top prize needed a longitude error of about 30 nautical miles. How far off was this watch?

hs003.text: But the Act's next part raised a new question.

hs004.text: What did one sea trial prove, and why build more clocks like it?

hs005.text: Harrison spent years on this watch. How would he answer the new terms?

hs006.text: The trial's problem: a ship sailing west finds no signposts for longitude out at sea.

hs007.text: But the sun passes overhead daily, and noon differs from place to place.

hs008.text: The Earth turns once in twenty-four hours; maps split that turn into 360 degrees.

hs009.text: Harrison put it plainly: one degree apart, noon differs by about four minutes.

hs010.text: The sun shows sailors the time where they are. And at the home port?

hs011.text: Harrison wanted a watch to take home-port time aboard and keep it at sea.

hs012.text: Compare the noon you see on board with the port time the watch kept, and you can work out how far east or west you've gone.

hs013.text: But ships roll and weather changes. Can a clock that runs on land hold up at sea?

hs014.text: So a 1714 Act offered a reward, putting every kind of method to trial at sea.

hs015.text: The reward had levels: the closer to the true position, the more money.

hs016.text: The top threshold we opened with carried a prize of £20,000.

hs017.text: So which clock did Harrison actually test?

hs018.text: Harrison built three timekeeping machines, then a fourth: a watch you could carry.

hs019.text: He kept the first three; they'd later enter the handover terms.

hs020.text: Not a wall pendulum clock on a ship; it had to beat the rolling of the sea.

hs021.text: After years of talks with the Board of Longitude, he won an official trial.

hs022.text: His son William went aboard. Could he bring the watch back safely?

hs023.text: William was sent to Portsmouth and waited a full five months for orders.

hs024.text: His father stayed ashore; the watch was by a ship about to sail.

hs025.text: Would a precise first trial win the top prize outright?

hs026.text: William took the watch aboard the Deptford, sailing from England to Jamaica.

hs027.text: He came back on another ship, bringing the watch home.

hs028.text: Then the star sightings and watch times were compared. Would both sides get one answer?

hs029.text: He had both places' observations too, and his figures differed.

hs030.text: Harrison wanted someone he trusted to check the sums; he recalls the Board refused.

hs031.text: Harrison's word alone can't settle who was wrong. What did Parliament record?

hs032.text: Harrison said he saw the Board's calculations only years later.

hs033.text: The Act's verdict was narrower: the watch was "of considerable use."

hs034.text: The Board first gave Harrison £2,500, to count toward any later prize.

hs035.text: But the top prize had not yet been formally awarded.

hs036.text: The first trial left a dispute. Would a second West Indies trip be clearer?

hs037.text: Harrison asked again; William sailed with the same watch.

hs038.text: This time he sailed from Portsmouth across the Atlantic to Bridgetown, Barbados.

hs039.text: The trial's results went to Parliament and into a new law.

hs040.text: With this watch, longitude was found within ten geographical miles, about ten nautical miles.

hs041.text: That's under the top prize's thirty, yet the Act didn't pay it all.

hs042.text: Harrison thought the trial settled the key question; Parliament set another hurdle.

hs043.text: One watch worked. Could other sea clocks be made just like it?

hs044.text: The Act first demanded the design.

hs045.text: The new Act split the top prize in two. What did the first half require?

hs046.text: Parliament said only a fully explained method and copies could make it widely usable.

hs047.text: The law gave him six months to explain his design's principles.

hs048.text: The first half: explain its construction, and give the Board the first three machines and this watch for public use.

hs049.text: The Jamaica money would come off the first half. And the other half?

hs050.text: The Act named no maker for copies, but the second half needed similar timekeepers.

hs051.text: The second half needed other such timekeepers made and tested within that threshold.

hs052.text: The Act didn't say how many, or how tests would end. How'd Harrison object?

hs053.text: Harrison said it was like changing the prize rules after the voyage was done.

hs054.text: Harrison said he opened the watch before the Board's men and explained it.

hs055.text: William handed the watch over; it left his father's hands.

hs056.text: Harrison said the first half was paid. Who would keep the watch?

hs057.text: Harrison said the Admiralty held it, then sent it to the Royal Observatory, Greenwich.

hs058.text: There, the watch began a test on land.

hs059.text: In 1766, Astronomer Royal Maskelyne took over, logging daily whether it ran fast or slow.

hs060.text: His published views angered Harrison. How would he respond?

hs061.text: Next year, Harrison printed a pamphlet attacking the method and the sums.

hs062.text: Harrison was disputing this very method: find the rate, then correct the time.

hs078.text: If it gains steadily, the known error can be taken off daily; but once adjusted, does the old rate hold?

hs063.text: Harrison said he changed its rate before handover, so the trial rate couldn't judge it.

hs064.text: That's his own rebuttal; the pamphlet alone can't prove the other side's test was wrong.

hs065.text: He asked the Board to lend the watch back for other makers to copy; he says it refused.

hs066.text: The fights over numbers and methods went into the pamphlet. Would Parliament pay again?

hs067.text: Years later, Parliament named Harrison in another Act.

hs068.text: The Act says he worked on sea timekeeping for forty-eight years.

hs069.text: Parliament said he'd made the principles public. Could more sea clocks be made?

hs070.text: The Act says yes: such timekeepers had been made, and kept good time.

hs079.text: But it doesn't list how far each later clock was off at sea, or who made them.

hs071.text: Parliament thought it would help navigation and trade, and allowed a new reward.

hs072.text: It authorized up to £8,750. Was this the original prize's second half?

hs073.text: The text calls it a "further reward," on top of what he'd received.

hs074.text: But it doesn't say what each half actually paid; the new sum can't reveal old accounts.

hs075.text: Finally, the Act had the Treasurer of the Navy pay this further reward.

hs076.text: If you were judging, would one sea trial do, or would you wait for copies?

hs077.text: Subscribe, and let's open history's question marks together.
